History The founding rally was planned for 200,000 people, and nearly a million came. The Second Regiment was unhappy with how the commune was made up and planned to mass on the east side of the rostrum and make trouble. Huang Jinhai moved several thousand people from Yangpu District in early to hold the east side. Pan Guoping was originally meant to chair the rally. See Huang Jinhai, Ten Years Not a Dream (《十年非梦》), ch. 7.

History On February 5 the Shanghai People's Commune was founded in People's Square. It adopted the declaration “Long Live the Victory of the January Revolution,” as revised by Zhang Chunqiao and Yao Wenyuan, and issued Order No. 1. Zhang Chunqiao was director, and Yao Wenyuan and Wang Hongwen were deputy directors. No election was ever held. The declaration says elections would wait until “after the victory of the all-round great power seizure,” and that for now the rebel organizations would form a three-in-one provisional committee “nominated through consultation.” It also contains the line “removed and purged at any time.” See the full text of the declaration on Wikisource. See Wikipedia, “January Storm,” Baidu Baike, “Shanghai People's Commune,” and Li Xun, “The Degeneration of Paris Commune Principles in the Cultural Revolution” (《巴黎公社原则在文革中的蜕变》) (search summary).

History Xu Jingxian's first draft of the commune declaration, following everyone's suggestions, included the Paris Commune principles described in The Civil War in France, such as “smash the state machine completely,” “commune committee members are elected directly by the masses” and “income may not exceed a worker's wages.” Zhang Chunqiao cut them all, and changed the title from “From the October Revolution to the January Revolution” to “Long Live the Victory of the January Revolution.” On the night of February 4, Zhang Chunqiao proposed calling the 38 constituent units sponsoring units, with nothing printed in the papers and no names signed, to calm a dispute among more than 600 organizations over status. See Li Xun, The Age of Revolutionary Rebellion (《革命造反年代》), ch. 20 (paraphrased).

History On February 12 Mao Zedong summoned Zhang Chunqiao and Yao Wenyuan to Beijing.

History The commune declaration itself promised elections. Leaders “will be elected by the revolutionary masses according to Paris Commune principles after the victory of the all-round great power seizure from the bottom up in Shanghai.” This dream only moves “later” forward to March.

Fiction This is the end of the Paris Commune dream (A1) in Act Two. Why did it not happen in history? Mao Zedong feared elections would shake the Party's leadership, and Zhang Chunqiao did not hold out. Who paid the price? The people who lost the elections, the people who were recalled, the shops whose output fell, and the one who held out at this table. How long it can last will only be known in Act Three. There it splits into three endings, military control, slow bureaucratization, or the first elected local government in the country.

History The Sixteen Points call for “a system of general elections like that of the Paris Commune.” Yet the Shanghai People's Commune never held an election. See Li Xun, “The Degeneration of Paris Commune Principles in the Cultural Revolution” (《巴黎公社原则在文革中的蜕变》).

History The commune declaration called for strict guard against organizations like the “Honorably Discharged Veterans” and the “Joint Action Committee.” “Once discovered, the organization is to be banned at once, and the chief culprits and those behind the scenes dealt with severely according to law.” The limits of association were written into the declaration on the day the commune was founded.

Fiction This is the end of the freedom of association dream (A2) in Act Two. Why did it not happen in history? The Six Articles on Public Security, published on January 13, 1967, made attacks on Mao Zedong and Lin Biao active counterrevolution. The limits of association were always drawn from above. History Article 87 of the 1954 Constitution gave citizens freedom of association. On November 14, 1966, Mao Zedong cited it in defense of WGHQ.

In history, the Scarlet Guards held preparatory meetings in the conference room of the Yangpu District Party Committee on November 23, 1966, and held their founding rally in People's Square on December 6 (Wikipedia gives November 26 as the founding date). On November 30 the Red Revolutionaries stormed the Liberation Daily building, and Workers' General Headquarters faced off with the Scarlet Guards for eight days and nine nights. On December 23 Cao Diqiu signed his acceptance of the Scarlet Guards' Eight Demands, and on the 25th he declared it void. On the 28th nearly 20,000 Scarlet Guards entered the Municipal Party Committee compound on Kangping Road to petition. In the early hours of the 30th they were scattered by WGHQ and other organizations. More than 300 were seized, 91 were badly injured, and the armbands were piled in six piles. That afternoon 10,000 Scarlet Guards set off north, and on the 31st they were stopped at Kunshan. On the 31st WGHQ issued the Extra-Urgent Order for the arrest of Scarlet Guard leaders.

On January 4 and 5, 1967, the rebels took over Wenhui Daily and Liberation Daily. On the 6th a rally in People's Square overthrew the Municipal Party Committee. On the 9th the Urgent Notice against economism was published, and on the 11th came the Center's message of congratulations. On the 19th Wang Hongwen called a meeting to prepare a new government. On February 5 the Shanghai People's Commune was founded, with Zhang Chunqiao as director and Wang Hongwen as deputy director. On February 12 Mao Zedong said, “we will still call it the revolutionary committee,” and on the 24th (the 23rd by one account) the name was changed. Around the 25th Geng Jinzhang was arrested, and the Second Regiment fell apart.

From Anting to the renaming was 106 days. A factory security officer became vice chairman of the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee.

1283: A notice issued by Workers' General Headquarters on February 11, 1967. It exposed Geng Jinzhang for building his own fiefdom and splitting the organization, announced that there would be no regiments under WGHQ, and barred any organization from forming regiments under the WGHQ banner. The next day Geng Jinzhang organized 110 trucks to parade through the city, shouting “Down with Wang Hongwen, down with Pan Guoping, down with Huang Jinhai.” On February 25 Geng Jinzhang was lured to the No. 31 State Cotton Mill and taken away.
1286: The Revolutionary Rebel Joint Headquarters of the Shanghai Diesel Engine Plant. The other faction in the plant was called The East Is Red. It had many Party members and middle-level cadres and followed Workers' General Headquarters. Liansi was mostly young workers and ordinary people. It also included people who had been persecuted in earlier campaigns, and some who had taken part in Scarlet Guard activities. In spring 1967 Liansi joined with the “Support-Liansi Station” outside the plant, called for a “second great upheaval” in Shanghai, and set up a platform for speeches in People's Square. In July Xie Fuxi, a section Party branch secretary from The East Is Red, was abducted by Liansi and beaten to death. After a rally in People's Square in the early hours of August 4, crowds surrounded the Shanghai Diesel plant and took the Liansi building. This became known as “smashing the Liansi.” It was the largest armed fighting in Shanghai's Cultural Revolution. In 1980 Workers' Daily said “983 people in the plant were beaten and injured.” Huang Jinhai thought this was exaggerated. The Special Court listed it as one of Wang Hongwen's crimes. It was also a battle of rebels against rebels, and both sides said they were the real rebels.
1288: The “Support-Liansi Liaison Station,” started in spring 1967 by Quan Xiangdong, a teaching assistant at Jiaotong University, and others. It brought together workers and students who opposed the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee and Workers' General Headquarters, under slogans like “power in the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee is not in proletarian hands” and “Shanghai must have a second great upheaval.” It included people who had been persecuted, people angry that the regiments had been abolished, former Scarlet Guards, and people who beat others under cover of the chaos. On July 31 WGHQ seized more than 30 of its leaders at once on Tai'an Road, and the Support-Liansi Station collapsed.
1290: Party branch secretary of a section in the tool shop of the Shanghai Diesel Engine Plant, and a member of The East Is Red. In July 1967 he was abducted by Liansi and beaten to death. According to the autopsy report Huang Jinhai kept, the body had 55 injuries large and small, “showing that the deceased was unable to resist.” Ye Yonglie's book cites a Liansi leaflet hinting that he died of heatstroke. His was the death before the smashing of the Liansi, and every side's account uses it to prove its own case.
1292: Twelfth Plenum of the Eighth Central Committee
1293: Held in Beijing from October 13 to 31, 1968. It passed a resolution to expel Liu Shaoqi “from the Party for good and dismiss him from all posts inside and outside the Party.” Wang Hongwen, as head of Shanghai's National Day delegation, was kept on to attend as a nonvoting participant. At the closing session on October 31, Mao Zedong told everyone present, “Let me introduce someone, this person is called Wang Hongwen, stand up and let us see you.” On the afternoon one head of state introduced a factory security officer to the whole room, another head of state was expelled from the Party for good.
1296: Held in April 1969. It wrote Lin Biao into the Party Constitution as Mao Zedong's successor. Wang Hongwen was elected a Central Committee member at 34.
1299: Political commissar of the Fourth Air Army and vice chairman of the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee. From 1968 he also headed Shanghai's military control commission for public security, procuratorate and courts. According to his posthumous manuscript, he refused to take in Scarlet Guards whom Workers' General Headquarters sent to be locked up, and he released cadres held by special case groups without real evidence, Chen Pixian among them. This made enemies of Zhang Chunqiao and Wang Hongwen. In March 1971 he attended the “Shanghai meeting” Lin Liguo called on Yueyang Road. On September 20 Xu Jingxian phoned to say Wang Hongwen invited him to the Jinjiang Hotel to read documents. When he arrived he was arrested by men Xu Shiyou had sent. In 1982 he was sentenced to 14 years. He died of illness in 1993. Wang Rui and Wikipedia both say he did not know of the Outline of Project 571 until he was put under isolation and investigation.
1302: Lin Biao's son, deputy director of the Air Force Operations Department. In 1971 he drafted the Outline of Project 571, which called Mao Zedong “B-52” and considered attacking Mao Zedong's special train near Shanghai. In March 1971 he called a meeting of air force commanders on Yueyang Road in Shanghai. On September 13 he fled by plane with Lin Biao, and the plane crashed at Undurkhan in Mongolia.
1305: On September 13, 1971, Lin Biao fled by plane and crashed in Mongolia. Before this Mao Zedong had been touring the south. On September 10 his special train stopped in Shanghai. He did not get off. He saw Xu Shiyou, Wang Hongwen and others on the train, then left ahead of schedule. After the incident the whole country hunted for “Lin Biao's sworn followers.” In Shanghai, Wang Weiguo was lured to the Jinjiang Hotel and arrested. For Wang Hongwen, it left the successor's place empty.
1307: Workers' Mao Zedong Thought Propaganda Team
1308: Formed from July 1968 out of workers and sent into schools, government offices and research units. On July 28 the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee set up a leading group for the Workers' Propaganda Teams, headed by Wang Hongwen. At one point the teams had 100,000 members. They were the most direct realization of the slogan of workers running universities and cultural units. They were also the face intellectuals saw most often in the ten years they were managed and struggled against.
1311: Commander of the Nanjing Military Region. In September 1971 he was ordered to handle the Lin Biao case in Shanghai, and worked with Wang Hongwen to lure Wang Weiguo into arrest.

1319: Yangshupu · Outside the No. 17 State Cotton Mill
1321:
The day after the “February 11 Notice” went out, Geng Jinzhang sent 110 trucks parading through the city. The people on the trucks shouted, down with Wang Hongwen, down with Pan Guoping, down with Huang Jinhai. The convoy drove to No. 31 Mill, then to No. 17 Mill, and circled twice outside the gate.

⟦0⟧

You watched from behind the window of the security section. You knew some of the faces on the trucks. ⟦1⟧ The streets were covered with his slogans, saying he wanted a big debate with you on television.

Some days earlier Huang Jinhai had sent two truckloads of people to smash the Second Regiment's office on Changshou Road. You had sent people to stop him, saying it was Comrade Chunqiao's view. Now word had come from Zhang Chunqiao again, and it meant the opposite. Geng Jinzhang claimed several hundred thousand people. He could no longer be controlled.

Huang Jinhai sat across from you, smoking. He said everyone under the Second Regiment thought they belonged to Workers' General Headquarters. Take down Geng Jinzhang alone and there would be no big trouble. He asked you, is this really Comrade Chunqiao's view or not, don't let it be like last time.
1322: They were people who had walked with you in Suzhou. One of them even waved at the window. You could not tell if it was at you or at someone else.
1323: They were people who had beaten you in the spearhead squad at Kunshan Middle School.
1324: They were people who had put on Second Regiment armbands after coming back from Suzhou.
1325: “It's Comrade Chunqiao's view,” you said. “I'm leaving this to you.”

History On February 11 Workers' General Headquarters issued a notice exposing Geng Jinzhang. The next day Geng Jinzhang organized a parade of 110 trucks. It circled twice outside No. 31 Mill and No. 17 Mill, and he demanded a television debate with Wang Hongwen. Earlier, Huang Jinhai had sent two truckloads of people to smash the Second Regiment's office on Changshou Road, and Wang Hongwen sent people to stop him, citing “Comrade Chunqiao's view.” Later Wang Hongwen told Huang Jinhai, “It's about time, we can arrest Geng Jinzhang.” Huang asked, “Does Zhang Chunqiao really agree to this or not? 1335: No. 31 State Cotton Mill · Jing'an District Cultural Center
1337:
You went to Zhabei alone. Geng Jinzhang saw you in his office, with the spearhead squad standing at the door. You said, come back, the Second Regiment's people belonged to Workers' General Headquarters all along. He heard you out and laughed. He said, Old Wang, you think I don't know who's standing behind you. As you walked out the door he said behind you, thank Comrade Chunqiao for me.

That afternoon he was still invited to No. 31 Mill. It was someone else who invited him.
1338: You called Geng Jinzhang and said you were waiting for him at No. 31 Mill to work out the television debate. He agreed at once.
1339: Huang Jinhai called Geng Jinzhang and said Wang Hongwen was waiting for him at No. 31 Mill to work out the television debate. He agreed at once.

In the afternoon three or four cars arrived. Geng Jinzhang came surrounded by followers, with the spearhead squad. Once he was inside, three of the four gates were shut, then the last one too. He asked, where's Wang Hongwen. Someone said upstairs. ⟦1⟧ Huang Jinhai blocked his way and argued with him. He lost his temper. Several strongmen rushed him and pushed him onto a truck. A few in the spearhead squad were from No. 31 Mill. When Huang Jinhai shouted, they stepped back. The truck drove to the Yangpu Public Security Sub-bureau, which had been told in advance.

That same evening you called the headquarters people to a meeting at the Jing'an District Cultural Center. Many people had been brought in from Luwan District. The room was tense. Nobody knew what the meeting was for.

The man you had to deal with was Fan Zuodong. In the most chaotic months at headquarters, he was the one who kept sitting there, answering phones, signing chits, clearing out the hangers-on. Some days earlier he and Workers' General Headquarters Standing Committee member Huang Wenhai had put up a notice saying any Standing Committee member who did not come to headquarters to work for three days would be struck off. Everyone knew who that was aimed at.

He sat in the third row with a notebook in his hand. He did not yet know the meeting was for him.
